questions.stem: After fertilisation, the zygote divides repeatedly as it travels along the oviduct. By the time it reaches the uterus, it is a ball of cells called a blastocyst. Why is it important that cell division begins before implantation?

options.text: The embryo must be large enough to attach to the thick uterus lining and receive nutrients
Cell division generates heat to keep the embryo warm during travel
The cells must be divided before the egg's food reserves run out completely
The zygote must become multicellular before it can begin producing its own DNA

questions.explanation: The zygote divides by mitosis to form a hollow ball of cells (blastocyst) during the 6-7 day journey to the uterus. This multicellular structure is needed for successful implantation into the uterus lining, where it can embed and establish connections to the mother's blood supply for nutrients and oxygen.

questions.stem: During fertilisation, the sperm's acrosome releases enzymes. What is the function of these enzymes?

options.text: They provide energy for the sperm tail to swim faster
They digest the protective layer around the egg, allowing the sperm nucleus to enter
They destroy competing sperm to ensure only one fertilises the egg
They cause the egg to start dividing immediately

questions.explanation: The acrosome at the tip of the sperm head contains digestive enzymes. During fertilisation, these enzymes are released to break down the zona pellucida (jelly-like protective layer) surrounding the egg cell. This allows the sperm to penetrate the egg and deliver its nucleus for fusion with the egg nucleus.

questions.stem: A zygote formed from fertilisation contains 46 chromosomes. How many chromosomes did each gamete contribute, and what type of cell division produced the gametes?

options.text: 23 from each gamete; gametes were produced by mitosis
46 from each gamete; gametes were produced by meiosis
23 from each gamete; gametes were produced by meiosis
23 from the sperm and 46 from the egg; the egg was produced by mitosis

questions.explanation: Gametes (sperm and egg) are produced by meiosis, which halves the chromosome number. Each human gamete contains 23 chromosomes (haploid). At fertilisation, the sperm nucleus (23) fuses with the egg nucleus (23), restoring the full diploid number of 46 chromosomes in the zygote.

questions.stem: An ectopic pregnancy occurs when the embryo implants in the oviduct instead of the uterus. Why is this dangerous?

options.text: The oviduct cannot provide blood or nutrients, so the embryo receives no food
The oviduct is too narrow to accommodate a growing embryo, which could rupture and cause life-threatening bleeding
The embryo will develop normally but be born prematurely
The oviduct is too cold for the embryo to develop properly

questions.explanation: The oviduct is a narrow tube not designed to support a growing pregnancy. As the embryo grows, it can cause the oviduct to stretch and eventually rupture, leading to severe internal bleeding that can be life-threatening. The uterus, by contrast, has a thick, stretchy muscular wall and a rich blood supply specifically adapted to support pregnancy.

questions.stem: After one sperm enters the egg, the egg's membrane changes rapidly to prevent other sperm from entering. What would happen if this mechanism failed and two sperm nuclei fused with the egg?

options.text: A normal embryo would develop with the same 46 chromosomes
The embryo would have 69 chromosomes, an abnormal number that usually prevents normal development
Identical twins would be produced
The extra sperm would be destroyed inside the egg without any effect

questions.explanation: If two sperm fertilised the same egg, the resulting cell would contain 23 + 23 + 23 = 69 chromosomes instead of the normal 46. This condition (triploidy) results in an abnormal number of chromosomes that almost always prevents normal embryonic development. The membrane change after fertilisation is therefore a critical mechanism for ensuring the correct chromosome number.
